questions.q: What does a logical gate like a Hadamard or CNOT actually reduce to on real hardware?
options: A fixed voltage that never changes regardless of which gate is applied
A permanent physical modification to the qubit's material structure
A purely digital instruction that requires no analog signal at all
A shaped analog microwave or laser pulse -- defined by amplitude, phase, frequency, and duration -- applied to a specific physical qubit (or pair of qubits)
questions.explain: Underneath the gate abstraction is an actual analog control pulse -- a microwave pulse for superconducting qubits or a laser pulse for trapped-ion/neutral-atom qubits -- calibrated with specific amplitude, phase, frequency, and duration.

questions.q: Why are control pulses calibrated per qubit rather than reused unmodified across an entire chip?
options: Because fabrication variation means no two physical qubits are identical, so each has its own resonant frequency and its own response to a drive pulse
Because pulses are only ever defined once for an entire chip and never adjusted afterward
Because providers intentionally restrict users from reusing pulse definitions for licensing reasons
Because every qubit on a chip is manufactured to be an exact, interchangeable copy, making per-qubit calibration unnecessary in practice
questions.explain: Real qubits vary chip to chip and qubit to qubit due to fabrication differences, so a pulse tuned for one qubit's frequency and response is not directly transferable to another without recalibration.

questions.q: What does pulse-level programming (e.g., OpenPulse / Qiskit Pulse-style access) let a user do that gate-level programming does not?
options: Specify the actual pulse shape directly -- envelope, phase, frequency, and timing -- bypassing the provider's default pre-calibrated gate implementation
Run circuits without any classical control electronics involved at all
Guarantee a lower error rate automatically with no additional calibration work
Eliminate the need for per-qubit calibration entirely
questions.explain: Pulse-level access exposes the raw control parameters below the fixed gate library, letting an advanced user or compiler define a custom pulse shape rather than relying on the provider's generic default -- at the cost of more work and more fragility.

questions.q: What problem does a DRAG (Derivative Removal by Adiabatic Gate) pulse specifically address on superconducting qubits?
options: Leakage -- the unwanted driving of population into a higher energy level outside the intended two-level qubit subspace -- which a DRAG pulse suppresses by adding a correction derived from the pulse's own envelope
The need for a dedicated readout amplifier on the signal return path
The complete elimination of all decoherence during a gate operation
The physical cooling of the qubit chip during gate execution
questions.explain: Real superconducting qubits aren't perfect two-level systems; a naive drive can leak population into a nearby higher state. DRAG pulses add an envelope-derived correction term that suppresses this leakage pathway, enabling faster or lower-error gates.

questions.q: Why might a provider's default, pre-calibrated gate not be optimal for a specific advanced use case, even though it has a published error rate?
options: Default gates are randomly generated and have no calibration process behind them at all
Published error rates for default gates are always fabricated and cannot be trusted
Default gates only work for single-qubit operations and never for two-qubit operations

The default pulse is tuned to perform well on average across typical use, not necessarily optimized for a specific circuit, a qubit's current state, or a tighter speed/fidelity trade-off than the default assumes
questions.explain: A provider's default pulse is calibrated to be broadly good, not specialized to any one use case -- which is exactly the gap that hand-tuned pulse-level control (like DRAG shaping) can close for a specific need, at the cost of extra effort and fragility.
